name: Grand Corridor
description:
Grand Boulevard was the beating heart of Bronzeville — the street where the Regal Theater stood, where the chess players gathered at the checkerboard, where Muddy Waters and Mahalia Jackson and a thousand other voices defined what American music would become. It was not just a neighborhood. It was a frequency. And when corporate sovereignty arrived, that frequency did not die. It went underground.

The surface of Grand Corridor is a Cinderblock AI residential district, an extension of the Bronzeline development — clean towers, tiered housing, compliance monitoring. Cinderblock acquired the old Bronzeville landmarks and preserved them as cultural assets: the former Regal Theater building is now a Waxwing Neuromedia immersive-experience venue where audiences can neural-share the memories of jazz performances from a century ago. The experience is extraordinary. It is also theft — the memories were harvested from elderly Bronzeville residents through a Waxwing program that offered free neural-interface installation in exchange for memory-access licensing. The residents did not understand what they were signing. Waxwing understood perfectly.

Beneath the corporate surface, the Grand Corridor's basements and sub-levels house the most important underground music scene in Meridian 88. The clubs operate in spaces that predate the sovereignty era — former speakeasies, storage basements, utility vaults — connected by passages that mirror the surface streets one level down. The music is live, unaugmented, played on instruments that do not require power and voices that do not require amplification. Neural-interface enhancement is prohibited in the underground clubs by unanimous consensus. The performers and audiences want the imperfect, human version of the sound. They want the crackle. They want the breath. They want the thing that Waxwing's memory-harvested immersive experiences cannot replicate because it was never a memory — it was a moment.

The cultural war between the surface and the underground defines Grand Corridor's daily life. Cinderblock and Waxwing profit from Bronzeville's heritage by packaging it as content. The underground preserves that heritage by practicing it, live, in the dark, for audiences that pay in cash and keep their mouths shut. The two economies coexist in the same district, separated by a floor. The corporate tenants upstairs attend Waxwing memory-share events and feel connected to history. The musicians downstairs play until their fingers bleed and feel connected to the future. Both are right. Neither will acknowledge the other.

King Drive still runs through the center of Grand Corridor, the Walk of Fame plaques continuing north from Bronzeline. But here, someone has been adding plaques — unauthorized bronze markers appearing overnight, commemorating people the official history left out. The janitors. The dishwashers. The women who cleaned the Regal Theater and hummed the songs while they swept. Cinderblock security removes them. They reappear. It has been happening for three years. Nobody knows who is making them.

sights: Corporate residential towers above, their lobbies decorated with Bronzeville memorabilia as corporate art
The Waxwing Neuromedia venue in the former Regal Theater building — historic facade, holographic marquee
Unauthorized Walk of Fame plaques appearing on King Drive, commemorating unnamed community members
Basement club entrances hidden behind service doors, marked with symbols only the initiated recognize
The contrast: curated heritage above, living culture below, separated by a single floor
sounds: Surface: Waxwing memory-share audio bleeding from the venue — ghosts of performances, technically perfect
Underground: live jazz, blues, and gospel from basement clubs — imperfect, breathing, human
The low rumble of the Cinderblock server farms that underlie the residential blocks
Foot traffic on King Drive — tourists by day, musicians by night, the sidewalk serving both
The sound of a saxophone through a basement ventilation grate — the underground leaking upward
smells: Underground club atmosphere: sweat, whiskey, the brass-and-reed smell of live instruments
Surface level: corporate-standard filtered air with Waxwing's branded scent overlay
The old smell of the underground passages — century-old brick, coal dust, the city's memory
Food from underground kitchen operations: cornbread, greens, catfish — soul food prepared in speakeasy conditions
atmosphere.feel: A district at war with itself over who owns its own history. Grand Corridor feels like standing between two speakers playing the same song in different keys — one pristine and recorded, one raw and live. The dissonance is the most honest sound in Meridian 88.

demographics: Surface: Tier 2-3 corporate residents, predominantly Cinderblock-affiliated. Underground: displaced Bronzeville community members, musicians, cultural preservationists. The underground population is uncounted — estimated at 3,000-5,000 operating in basement-level spaces throughout the district.
economy: Waxwing Neuromedia's memory-share venue generates the district's primary corporate revenue. Cinderblock's residential management provides supplementary income. The underground club economy operates on cash, barter, and the social currency of cultural authenticity. Soul food from underground kitchens commands premium prices from those who know where to find it.
power_structure: Cinderblock AI and Waxwing Neuromedia share corporate jurisdiction. The underground music scene is governed by a loose confederation of club operators and elder musicians whose authority derives from cultural respect, not force. The two power structures coexist by mutual ignorance — the corporations know the underground exists but find it easier to pretend otherwise.
dangers: Waxwing's memory-harvesting program continues to target elderly residents with exploitative licensing agreements
Underground clubs risk corporate raids — discovery would end the scene and displace the community again
Cinderblock surveillance in the residential blocks makes surface-to-underground movement risky
The unauthorized Walk of Fame plaques have become a political flashpoint — Cinderblock security is escalating enforcement
Cultural erasure: the corporate version of Bronzeville's history is slowly replacing the real one in public memory
opportunities: The underground club network is an information exchange disguised as entertainment
Waxwing's memory-harvesting technology, if stolen, has applications that would interest every faction in M88
The unauthorized plaque-maker is a folk hero — finding and protecting them would earn significant community loyalty
Underground soul food operations need supply chain support from districts like Little Furnace
The cultural war generates demand for intermediaries who can move between surface and underground
story_hooks: Waxwing Neuromedia has discovered that its memory-share recordings contain something unexpected — the harvested memories include experiences that the donors could not have had, as if the memories themselves have been growing, adding scenes that never happened, and the Regal Theater venue is showing audiences visions of events that have not occurred yet

The unauthorized plaque-maker has been identified — she is a Cinderblock employee working in the residential management office, and she has been using corporate fabrication equipment to make the plaques on her night shift, and she has just made one with Kyle's name on it

An underground club has received a challenge: a Waxwing-sponsored performer wants to play a live set in the basement venue, unaugmented, to prove that the corporate version of the music can match the underground. The club scene is divided — some see an opportunity for exposure, others see the beginning of co-optation
frequented_by: Underground musicians maintaining Bronzeville's live performance tradition
Waxwing memory-share audiences experiencing curated cultural heritage
Displaced Bronzeville community members returning for underground club nights
Information traders using the club network as a social exchange
Cultural tourists on King Drive, unaware of what is happening beneath their feet
